subject: English
passage: The Song of the Lark is a 1915 novel by Willa Cather set in the American West and in Chicago in the late nineteenth century. In the novel, Thea Kronborg attends a musical soiree. Thea compares her musical talent favorably to that of other young singers from Chicago's drawing-room circles who are performing that evening: ______
prompt: Which quotation from The Song of the Lark best illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "It puzzled [Thea] that the drawing-room should hum along just as before, when her own feelings toward it had grown so utterly different."
choices.B: "Thea Kronborg felt herself distinctly the superior of these favored pupils of Chicago's drawing-room circles; she had probably practiced more, studied more, and even sung before harder audiences, than any other singer in the room."
choices.C: "No trouble had been spared on the arrangements, which were admitted to be very tasteful even by guests who shared [Thea's] familiarity with the concert halls of Berlin and New York."
choices.D: "Singly [the singers around Thea] betrayed their limitations; but taken together they stood for 'Chicago,' and the force of social custom made her defer to their verdict on all matters deemed respectable."

explanation:
Choice B is the best answer because it most effectively illustrates the claim that Thea compares her musical talent favorably to that of other young singers. The quotation explicitly states that Thea felt herself 'distinctly the superior of these favored pupils of Chicago's drawing-room circles' and that 'she had probably practiced more, studied more, and even sung before harder audiences, than any other singer in the room.' This directly demonstrates Thea's favorable comparison of her own musical talent to that of the other performers.

Why D is incorrect:

Choice D is incorrect because while this quotation does mention that the singers 'betrayed their limitations,' it does not effectively illustrate the claim about musical comparison. The quotation instead focuses on how the singers collectively stood for 'Chicago' and influenced Thea's deference to their verdict on respectable matters through social custom.
